At school he discovered that spreadsheet exercises were less irritating than essays. He could enter batches of information accurately if the source was clear. He rarely volunteered this fact in conversations about his future. His father wanted him to become more ambitious and compared him with a cousin. Luis answered with silence or sarcasm, and neither changed the other's position.

At sixteen he still follows football closely and sees one friend occasionally, but has few other chosen activities. He arrives late when he oversleeps or misses the first bus connection. His laundry supervisor trusts him with opening checklists when another adult is present. He says a predictable indoor job sounds fine, though he has not sought information about any particular role.

demonstratedSkills: Maintains familiar cleaning standards without repeated reminders
ambitions: Wants his own room or place when affordable
Would consider regular indoor work; no settled direction
supports: One school office worker notices absences
practicalConstraints: Shared bedroom area near household activity
No family budget for exploratory travel

selfDescription: I don't need everything to be exciting. At work I know what has to get done and then I leave. School has stuff missing from last month that comes back again, so it never feels finished. My dad says I act like I don't care. I care about some things. I just don't want to tell him a plan so he can explain why it's not enough.
openQuestions: Would routine administrative work hold his interest outside a familiar setting?
What contributes most to his lateness: sleep, transport, or reluctance to attend?
What choices would he make if comparison with relatives were removed?

name: Audrey Whitfield

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger brother; parents are attentive, busy, and highly involved in choices; conflict over dating and privacy remains unresolved.
background.finances: Affluent household with private tuition, travel, and paid enrichment available.
background.geography: Austin, Texas; family spends part of each summer with relatives in Colorado.
background.cultureLanguages: White American; English at home; nominal church affiliation, most social life through school families.
background.school: Small college-preparatory private high school; consistently good grades with substantial tutoring and scheduling support.
background.accessOpportunities: Extensive organized opportunities and reliable transport, but very little unsupervised exploration or paid work.

timeline.story: Audrey's days were arranged around preschool, swimming lessons, and appointments written on a kitchen calendar. She liked sticker books and telling adults what her younger brother was doing wrong. Her parents took many photographs and praised her willingness to smile. She enjoyed familiar visitors but became restless on museum trips chosen because adults thought they would be enriching.

She attended a small private elementary school where most children knew each other outside class. She learned how to follow classroom expectations and earned frequent good-behavior marks. Her mother tried piano lessons, tennis, and a children's art class. Audrey did not hate them, but she rarely asked to continue once the scheduled session ended or the equipment was put away.

A tutor helped her prepare spelling and math work twice a week. Audrey liked having someone explain exactly what would be assessed. She spent sleepovers making up rankings of favorite outfits and celebrities. A quieter classmate sometimes became the subject of the group's jokes. Audrey usually laughed along and has never considered herself the person who started them.

Remote school took place in a dedicated room with a reliable laptop. Her parents organized virtual activities when she complained of boredom. Audrey preferred chatting privately with friends while the official activity ran. She became very familiar with the appearance of other families' homes on camera and began noticing which possessions signaled that someone belonged in her social circle.

She returned to a school that talked frequently about leadership and future applications. Audrey joined clubs her friends joined and accepted a minor title that required almost no work. She received praise for a polished presentation after a tutor helped structure it. She knew the final result looked good but could not say which part she had actually enjoyed producing.

A relationship with a boy at another school occupied more thought than her classes. Her parents wanted access to her messages after she lied about where a group was meeting. Audrey viewed their response as humiliating; they viewed her refusal to explain as proof of poor judgment. The rules tightened, and she became more skilled at giving technically true, incomplete answers.

At sixteen she earns good grades, tracks deadlines carefully, and spends considerable time maintaining group chats and browsing resale clothes. She has no sustained hobby outside those social routines. Her parents discuss selective colleges as a shared family project. Audrey wants to go somewhere they cannot visit without planning, but has not separated that desire from interest in any course of study.

avoids: Activities none of her friends attend
activities: School social committees with limited duties
Weekend outings arranged with parental permission
ambitions: Wants to attend college away from home
Has no settled academic interest despite naming impressive options in adult conversations
practicalConstraints: Little experience managing everyday responsibilities independently

selfDescription: I know I'm lucky. Everybody reminds me, especially if I complain. I can be lucky and still want to do one thing without explaining it first. I don't know what my favorite subject is. Usually it's whichever teacher makes it clear how to get a good grade. My friends all sound like they have plans, but sometimes I think we're just saying what we said last time.
openQuestions: What would she choose without a friend or parent selecting the initial options?
Which demonstrated strengths transfer when tutoring and reminders decrease?
Will distance from home clarify her interests or mainly relieve conflict?

name: Darius Bell

background.family: Lives with his father, an aunt, and two cousins; mother died when he was three, and family speaks about her openly without making every milestone about the loss.
background.finances: Stable lower-middle-income household; adults share expenses and plan large purchases.
background.geography: Beaumont, Texas; several relatives live within a short drive.
background.cultureLanguages: Black American; English at home; family fishing trips and church meals provide regular social contact.
background.school: Public high school; generally solid grades, quiet participation, strong engagement in one laboratory elective.
background.accessOpportunities: School laboratory facilities, a community aquarium group, library resources, and adult support for inexpensive projects.

timeline.story: Darius spent preschool afternoons at his aunt's kitchen table drawing loops while older cousins did homework. He liked the hum of her aquarium filter and watched the fish longer than anyone expected. His father answered questions about his mother when they arose. Most days were ordinary: snacks, arguments over television, and someone reminding him to put his shoes away.

He entered school quietly and was sometimes overlooked when louder classmates volunteered. He liked counting objects and explaining rules to one friend at a time. Reading aloud made him tense even when he knew the passage. At home he helped feed the fish with close supervision because his aunt had explained that extra food could make the tank worse.

At eight he received a small secondhand tank and spent more time choosing stones than researching equipment. His aunt insisted they learn the basics before adding fish. He found the waiting frustrating. Once the tank was established, he kept the same simple routine for months, checking it after school before watching television or playing a familiar racing game.

A tank developed cloudy water, and Darius and his aunt compared several possible causes using library information and a basic test kit. Some readings confused them. They asked a local aquarium-group member rather than guessing repeatedly. Darius enjoyed keeping numbers in a notebook, although he sometimes wrote only that the water looked fine when he was impatient to do something else.

In middle school he grew taller quickly and became embarrassed when adults repeatedly suggested basketball. He did not enjoy playing and disliked disappointing them. His closest friend moved across town, so they maintained a quiet friendship through games and occasional visits. Darius found a new lunch seat eventually, but did not feel a need to become part of a large group.

A school laboratory elective introduced him to pH measurements and comparisons among water samples. Familiarity with his tank helped him ask specific questions without making him good at every science task. He struggled to use the microscope at first and disliked being rushed by a partner. His teacher noticed his orderly notes and asked him to demonstrate a measurement routine privately.

At sixteen Darius still maintains the aquarium and is helping compare school tap-water samples collected at different times using approved classroom methods. He likes repeated measurement and modest questions with checkable results. He has never designed a large investigation alone. His father encourages further education without naming a profession. Darius worries that being quiet will make people think he has nothing to contribute.

activities: Occasional aquarium-group meetings with his aunt
demonstratedSkills: Recognizes changes from a familiar baseline
Asks for clarification before changing procedures
motivations: Being trusted without being put on display
ambitions: Wants to continue learning about water and living systems
Has not chosen a future role or institution
struggles: Impatience when others rush careful work

selfDescription: I don't talk a lot in class because somebody usually answers before I'm ready. At home I talk plenty. I like checking something again and finding out if it's really different or if it just looked different yesterday. People hear fish and think I want a giant tank or a fish business. I mostly like the one I have. I haven't thought that far ahead.
openQuestions: Will he enjoy broader scientific questions beyond his aquarium context?
What settings allow him to demonstrate knowledge without rushing?
Does he want a larger social role or simply recognition of his current contributions?

name: Valentina Salazar

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger brother; grandmother lives in the same duplex; family sometimes disagrees about how much help to offer.
background.finances: Stable working-class household; discretionary spending is limited but essentials and school supports are covered.
background.geography: El Paso, Texas; extended family ties in Ciudad Juárez.
background.cultureLanguages: Mexican American; uses spoken English and Spanish, written messaging, and some ASL; bilateral hearing loss identified in early childhood, with hearing aids and school accommodations.
background.school: Public magnet high school; uses captioning and preferential seating; average-to-good grades.
background.accessOpportunities: School business course, accessible library programming, home phone and laptop; group activities vary in how well access needs are met.

timeline.story: Valentina liked covering the kitchen floor with pretend restaurant menus and assigning adults the same order repeatedly. Her family learned about her hearing loss after noticing missed responses in noisy rooms. Hearing aids and appointments became part of the household schedule. She still wanted the red cup, argued over bedtime, and preferred being read the same picture book every night.

In elementary school she learned to tell teachers when she could not follow an instruction. Adults sometimes praised this so enthusiastically that she wished they would move on. She liked drawing price tags and playing shop with a neighbor. At birthday parties she often understood the game after watching a round, although overlapping voices could make the jokes difficult to catch.

Her grandmother taught her simple sewing repairs, which Valentina tolerated because she wanted to alter doll clothes. The interest did not grow into a lasting sewing hobby. She preferred making short videos with cousins and adding exaggerated captions. At school she enjoyed straightforward arithmetic and became annoyed when classmates assumed a missed comment meant she did not understand the whole lesson.

Remote learning made some things easier because written instructions stayed on screen. Poor automatic captions created other problems. Valentina became quick at asking classmates to send the actual assignment wording. She spent considerable time in group chats discussing shows and classmates. Her parents thought she was studying more than she was because she almost always had the laptop open.

She entered a magnet program after her mother encouraged the application. Valentina liked the new building and initially regretted leaving neighborhood friends. She started browsing resale listings and noticed how photographs, descriptions, and response times affected which items sold. She sold a few outgrown clothes with parental supervision, enjoying the listing process more than arranging pickup with unfamiliar buyers.

A business applications class introduced her to inventory tables and simple cost comparisons. She liked organizing information for an actual small sale. Group discussions remained tiring when classmates spoke over one another, and she sometimes withdrew even after the teacher offered help. She had a brief relationship with a classmate who messaged constantly; she ended it because she wanted fewer demands on her time.

At sixteen Valentina manages a small monthly resale listing session with a cousin and keeps a simple record of costs and proceeds. She does not consider it a growing business yet. She likes clothes and social media but sometimes takes a week away from posting. Her family encourages a secure degree; she wants to compare ordinary work settings before agreeing that more school is the obvious next step.

avoids: Customers who send repeated vague messages
Being treated as a lesson about perseverance
demonstratedSkills: Maintains simple inventory and proceeds records
motivations: Being considered capable without excessive attention
ambitions: Wants to experience several ordinary workplaces
Could imagine continued study but has not chosen a subject
struggles: Occasional withdrawal instead of requesting clarification

selfDescription: I like making a listing look clear. I don't need to make a brand out of everything. Sometimes I just want the old jeans out of the closet. At school I want people to repeat the thing I missed and then keep talking normally. My family worries about people being rude. People can be rude, but that's not the only thing I think about when I choose where to go.
openQuestions: Does she prefer organizing sales or the clothing itself?
Which workplace communication conditions matter most to her?
How much independence does she want to take on next?

name: Beck Hollis

background.family: Lives with maternal grandparents and a younger sibling; mother works in another city and visits irregularly; disagreements about identity and household expectations remain active.
background.finances: Grandparents cover necessities through retirement income and part-time work; little extra money.
background.geography: Small town outside Wichita Falls, Texas; previously lived in three other North Texas towns.
background.cultureLanguages: White American; English-speaking; nonbinary, with consistent pronoun use at school and mixed responses among relatives.
background.school: Small public high school; good attendance, average grades, prefers practical tasks to essays.
background.accessOpportunities: Library computer access, school weather station, and a volunteer preparedness club; opportunities require local availability or shared rides.

timeline.story: Beck remembered early homes by the sound of the refrigerator and where the dog slept. Their mother changed apartments several times for work and rent. Grandparents provided a familiar place on many weekends. Beck liked watching the sky from the porch and asking whether a dark cloud meant rain. They were just as interested in biscuits and cartoons afterward.

Starting school, Beck liked classroom jobs with a visible result, such as stacking chairs or carrying a folder to the office. They disliked drawing a picture of a future family when the teacher specified what it should contain. A neighbor child became a close friend through shared bus rides. Most play involved bikes, sidewalk games, and negotiating whose turn it was to choose.

Beck and their sibling began staying mostly with their grandparents. The adults described the arrangement as temporary for several years. Beck learned to pack a school bag the night before because their grandmother insisted, not because they were naturally organized. They enjoyed weather maps on television and could identify approaching storm areas on the screen without understanding much of the underlying science.

A severe-weather drill at school prompted Beck to ask why different rooms had different shelter instructions. A custodian explained practical details about windows and interior walls. Beck remembered the explanation and repeated it at home. They also became absorbed in a cooperative online game with their bus friend, often arguing about strategy and staying up later than their grandparents allowed.

Beck began using a different name with friends and later asked school staff to use they/them pronouns. Their grandmother tried, while their grandfather often avoided pronouns entirely and complained about corrections. Meals became tense when the subject arose. Beck continued doing chores and watching television with him, but the disagreement did not turn into a clear story of reconciliation.

A teacher invited Beck to help check a simple school weather station. They liked cleaning the rain gauge, recording readings, and noticing when equipment had stopped updating. Through the same teacher they joined a small preparedness club, assembling supply bins and practicing clear messages. They did not enjoy the public demonstration day, when strangers expected cheerful explanations and photographs.

At sixteen Beck helps maintain a list of club supplies and participates in supervised practice exercises. They have never responded to an actual emergency. A close friend now spends more time with a romantic partner, leaving Beck lonely on weekends. They want a future with predictable housing and some choice about their schedule, but currently know more about local routines than wider possibilities.

motivations: Friendship that does not depend on being entertaining
ambitions: Wants to finish school and live somewhere stable
Interested in practical outdoor and team tasks without a settled plan
supports: Teacher includes them in practical tasks
One longstanding friend despite reduced time together

selfDescription: I like weather because it is always doing something, even if people say nothing is happening. I don't want every conversation about me to become a conversation about my name. I can do a checklist and I usually remember to show up. That doesn't mean I know what I want forever. Mostly I want next year to feel less crowded with everybody else's decisions.
openQuestions: Which practical activities would interest them beyond local school opportunities?
How will they build companionship as their closest friendship changes?
What does stable independent living require in the settings they might consider?
